items.prompt: A fleet is patched manually in place and now has inconsistent packages. Which change improves reliability?
constraints: Instances can be replaced.
The desired image can be built and tested.
Rollback must use a known artifact.

options.text: Build a versioned immutable image, test it, launch replacement instances from that artifact, and remove the old version through a controlled rollout.
Patch each instance differently until the fleet's behavior appears consistent in production.
Keep manual changes undocumented because immutable images prevent emergency fixes.
Restart the load balancer so its targets automatically receive the new packages.

feedback.Reason: Immutable replacement creates a repeatable fleet state and makes rollback to a known artifact possible.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A versioned image or container artifact is built once and deployed consistently to replace mutable hosts.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team tests the artifact, refreshes instances in batches, observes health, and retains the prior version for rollback.
Details.errorCorrection: In-place drift is hard to reproduce, undocumented emergency changes become future drift, and a load balancer does not patch targets.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Immutable rollout needs build, artifact retention, and deployment automation but reduces configuration drift.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Different manual changes increase drift and make failures difficult to reproduce.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Emergency fixes still need versioning and promotion into the canonical artifact path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Load balancers route traffic and do not update host packages.

items.prompt: A release needs instant traffic reversal if the new version fails, and both versions can run concurrently. Which deployment pattern fits?
constraints: The old environment remains available.
Traffic can switch through a controlled endpoint.
State migrations are backward compatible or separately coordinated.

options.text: Use blue/green environments with a tested traffic switch, health validation, compatible data changes, and a rollback path to the green environment.
Overwrite the only environment in place and keep a screenshot of the previous configuration.
Switch traffic before the new environment has passed health and dependency tests.
Delete the old environment immediately so the new version cannot be compared.

feedback.Reason: Blue/green keeps a known-good environment available while the new environment is validated and traffic is switched deliberately.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Two independently deployable environments allow controlled routing and rapid rollback when application and data contracts are compatible.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team tests the new color, shifts traffic gradually or atomically, and retains the old color until rollback risk passes.
Details.errorCorrection: In-place overwrite removes the rollback boundary, untested traffic switch expands risk, and deleting the old environment removes recovery.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Running two environments costs more and requires data migration discipline.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A screenshot is not a deployable rollback artifact.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Unvalidated traffic exposes users to unknown failure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Removing the known-good environment eliminates the quickest rollback path.

items.prompt: A message can be delivered twice to different workers after a timeout. Which property prevents an incorrect duplicate outcome?
constraints: At-least-once delivery is possible.
The operation has a stable business key.
Workers can access a durable record of completion.

options.text: Make the command idempotent with a durable deduplication or idempotency record and an atomic business-state transition.
Assume a distributed queue delivers every message exactly once in all failure cases.
Use the worker hostname as the deduplication key because hosts are unique.
Acknowledge before the business transition so duplicate delivery cannot occur.

feedback.Reason: Distributed retries and duplicate delivery are handled by an idempotent business boundary, not by host identity or early acknowledgment.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A stable operation key and durable completion record allow a duplicate to return the prior result or avoid repeating the side effect.
Details.scenarioApplication: Workers can be replaced or run concurrently without charging, provisioning, or publishing the same business result twice.
Details.errorCorrection: Delivery guarantees do not remove all duplicate outcomes, hostnames are replaceable, and early acknowledgment can lose work.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Deduplication storage needs retention and concurrency rules aligned with the business operation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Retries and ambiguous failures can still produce duplicate delivery or effects.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Worker identity does not identify the business operation across replacement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Acknowledging before completion removes the work from recovery and does not prevent an already-running duplicate.

items.prompt: A schema change must work while old and new application versions run during a rolling deployment. Which migration style is safer?
constraints: Mixed versions can coexist temporarily.
The old version must continue serving.
Rollback must not require destructive schema reversal.

options.text: Use an expand-and-contract migration: add backward-compatible structures, deploy readers and writers safely, migrate data, then remove the old structure after cutover.
Drop the old column before deploying the new application so no version can use it.
Deploy the new application first and assume old instances will ignore incompatible schema changes.
Change the schema manually on one replica and let replication resolve application compatibility.

feedback.Reason: Backward-compatible schema evolution preserves service availability during mixed-version deployment and rollback.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Expand-and-contract separates adding compatible state from migrating readers and removing old state after all consumers move.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team tests old and new versions together and retains the old structure until rollback is no longer required.
Details.errorCorrection: Dropping first breaks old versions, assuming compatibility is unsafe, and one replica cannot define canonical schema migration.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The transition temporarily maintains duplicate fields or code but converges to one canonical schema after evidence.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Old code can fail immediately when its required column is removed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Mixed-version compatibility must be designed and tested, not assumed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Manual replica changes can create drift and do not define authoritative schema ownership.

items.prompt: A container service deploys an image tag named latest, and different tasks pull different bytes. Which change improves determinism?
constraints: Deployments must be reproducible.
Rollback needs a known image.
Tasks can be replaced automatically.

options.text: Publish immutable, content-addressed or versioned image tags, pin the task definition to the chosen artifact, and roll out through a controlled deployment.
Keep using latest and restart tasks until all of them happen to pull the same image.
Copy the image bytes into every task's writable filesystem and treat the task as the registry.
Use the load balancer target name as the image version because target names are stable.

feedback.Reason: Pinned immutable artifacts prevent a deployment from depending on mutable registry labels or task timing.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A task definition references a known image version or digest so replacement tasks run the same artifact.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team verifies the image, deploys a new task definition, observes target health, and can restore the prior definition.
Details.errorCorrection: Restart timing does not make latest deterministic, task filesystems are not registry authority, and target names do not version images.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Artifact retention and promotion policies add governance but improve rollback and auditability.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Mutable tags can resolve to different image content during a rollout.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Task-local copies disappear with replacement and do not provide shared artifact authority.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Target identity is traffic routing metadata, not image provenance.

items.prompt: A producer can create work faster than consumers can process it. Which distributed pattern protects availability?
constraints: Work can wait with a defined freshness bound.
Consumers have finite downstream capacity.
Messages must not be silently dropped.

options.text: Use a durable queue, bounded consumer concurrency, visibility and retry controls, dead-letter handling, and queue-age alarms as backpressure.
Let producers call every consumer synchronously until one accepts the work.
Increase producer retries without delay so the queue drains faster.
Drop the oldest messages silently whenever queue depth rises.

feedback.Reason: A queue absorbs a bounded rate mismatch while consumer limits and retry controls protect downstream systems.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Durable buffering separates arrival from processing; visibility, idempotency, and DLQ isolate failed work.
Details.scenarioApplication: The service admits work, monitors queue age, scales consumers within quotas, and exposes an explicit stale or rejected state when the bound is exceeded.
Details.errorCorrection: Synchronous fan-out couples producer availability, immediate retries amplify overload, and silent drops destroy work.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Queueing increases completion latency and requires retention and poison-message policies.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Synchronous consumers make the producer depend on every consumer's availability.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: No-delay retries increase pressure rather than processing capacity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Silent dropping violates the durability and product contract.

items.prompt: A downstream consumer loses its local projection, but the source event history is retained. Which recovery pattern is appropriate?
constraints: Events are immutable or append-only.
The consumer projection is derived.
Replay must be idempotent and bounded.

options.text: Rebuild the projection by replaying the authoritative event history with a versioned consumer, checkpointing, idempotent handlers, and a cutover validation.
Treat the projection as authoritative and discard the event history to avoid duplicate processing.
Replay events concurrently without ordering or deduplication because derived state can be rebuilt arbitrarily.
Return the empty projection as successful data until a user reports a missing record.

feedback.Reason: An immutable event history can reconstruct a derived projection when replay is controlled and handlers are safe to repeat.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Events remain the source for the projection; checkpoints, ordering where required, and idempotency make replay recoverable.
Details.scenarioApplication: The consumer builds a new projection, compares counts and invariants, and switches reads only after validation.
Details.errorCorrection: A derived projection is not authority, uncoordinated replay can corrupt state, and empty success hides recovery failure.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Event retention and replay time add storage and operational cost but provide a durable recovery path.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A derived projection is not the durable source if it can be rebuilt from history.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Replay still needs ordering, deduplication, and business conflict rules.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Returning empty data creates a silent correctness failure.

items.prompt: A production bug is found in the current image, and the team wants a fast rollback. What must already exist?
constraints: The previous version is known-good.
Rollback must be repeatable.
State changes are compatible with the previous version or separately reversible.

options.text: Retain the prior immutable artifact and deployment configuration, and test that traffic can return to it without losing or corrupting state.
Rebuild the previous version from memory during the incident.
Keep only the current artifact because storing old images increases storage cost.
Rollback by manually undoing package changes on the same hosts.

feedback.Reason: Immutable retained artifacts make rollback a known deployment action rather than an emergency reconstruction.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Versioned images, task definitions, templates, and compatible data migrations allow a previous service version to be redeployed consistently.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team promotes the prior artifact, monitors health, and preserves the failed version for investigation without using it for serving.
Details.errorCorrection: Incident reconstruction is slow and error-prone, deleting artifacts removes recovery, and mutable host undo preserves drift.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Artifact retention has storage cost but supports recovery, audit, and incident diagnosis.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Reconstructing an artifact during failure increases time and uncertainty.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Deleting rollback artifacts trades storage savings for recovery risk.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Manual undo is difficult to reproduce and can leave inconsistent hosts.

items.prompt: An order status projection may lag the transactional source by seconds. Which product behavior makes the distributed design safe?
constraints: The source remains authoritative.
The UI can show pending or last-updated state.
Users must not be told an uncommitted status is final.

options.text: Expose an explicit freshness or pending state, define the projection lag objective, and use the source for decisions that require current transactional truth.
Hide the lag and label every projection as current so users never see eventual consistency.
Make every read wait indefinitely for all projections to converge.
Let the projection become the write authority because it is optimized for reads.

feedback.Reason: Eventual consistency is safe when the product and service contracts distinguish derived freshness from authoritative state.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The application communicates pending or last-updated state and routes critical decisions to the transactional owner.
Details.scenarioApplication: Users can see that a projection is catching up, while order authorization or settlement reads current source state.
Details.errorCorrection: Hiding lag misleads users, indefinite waits harm availability, and a read projection should not own writes by default.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Explicit eventual consistency can increase UI complexity but improves availability and independent scaling.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Mislabeling stale state can cause incorrect user decisions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Waiting indefinitely turns bounded lag into an availability failure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A derived read model should not silently become the canonical write owner.

items.prompt: Two workers must not process the same exclusive lease, but the lock service can fail. Which design avoids an unsafe permanent lock?
constraints: Work can be retried after a timeout.
A lock holder can crash.
The service must define lease expiry and fencing.

options.text: Use a bounded lease with renewal and fencing or version checks, persist work state, and make the business operation idempotent or transactionally protected.
Use a lock with no expiry so a crashed worker never shares work.
Use the worker process memory as the lock record because it is fastest.
Ignore lock failure and let both workers write because duplicate work is harmless for every operation.

feedback.Reason: Distributed locks must recover from holder failure and prevent stale holders from committing after their lease expires.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Leases expire, fencing tokens or versions reject stale writes, and durable work state supports recovery.
Details.scenarioApplication: A crashed worker does not block work forever, and a delayed old worker cannot overwrite a newer owner.
Details.errorCorrection: No-expiry locks deadlock, process memory is not shared durable authority, and duplicate writes can violate business correctness.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Lease duration and renewal add timing sensitivity, so clocks, retries, and fencing must be tested.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A crashed holder can leave an unexpired or permanent lock and block recovery.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Local memory cannot coordinate independent workers.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Duplicate work is not universally harmless and must be handled explicitly.

items.prompt: A corrupted host is causing errors in one Availability Zone. Why is replacement safer than manual repair when the image is known-good?
constraints: The host is disposable.
The image and configuration are versioned.
State is stored outside the host.

options.text: Replace the host from the known-good artifact, drain traffic, validate health, and preserve logs or snapshots separately for diagnosis.
Repair packages manually on the host and never record the change so replacement is avoided.
Copy the corrupted host into a new image so the new fleet reproduces its state.
Leave the host in service and add retries so users compensate for its corruption.

feedback.Reason: Immutable replacement returns disposable compute to a known state while preserving diagnostic evidence outside the serving host.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The artifact and automation reproduce the desired configuration; logs and snapshots retain evidence without making corrupted state canonical.
Details.scenarioApplication: Traffic drains, a replacement becomes healthy, and the old host is isolated for investigation or forensic retention.
Details.errorCorrection: Manual repair creates drift, copying corruption spreads it, and retries do not remove an unhealthy target.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Replacement can lose local diagnostics unless logs are externalized, so observability is part of immutability.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Undocumented repair creates drift and makes future replacements inconsistent.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A corrupted host is not a safe source for a new immutable artifact.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Retries can amplify load and do not fix the failed target.

items.prompt: A service has three nested retrying layers and becomes unavailable during a downstream slowdown. Which correction is most important?
constraints: Each layer can retry.
The dependency is already slow.
The end-to-end request has a bounded deadline.

options.text: Set one end-to-end retry or deadline budget, make retries bounded and jittered, and prevent every layer from independently multiplying attempts.
Increase retries at every layer because more attempts always improve eventual success.
Remove all timeouts so a request can wait for the dependency to recover.
Return a successful empty result whenever a retry budget is exhausted.

feedback.Reason: Distributed retries multiply load and can turn a dependency slowdown into a broad outage without a shared budget.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A deadline and bounded retry policy preserve caller capacity and prevent nested attempts from exceeding downstream limits.
Details.scenarioApplication: The service records attempts and exposes a clear unavailable or asynchronous outcome when the budget is exhausted.
Details.errorCorrection: More retries can create a retry storm, unbounded waits exhaust threads, and fake success hides missing data.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Fewer retries may reduce eventual success for transient faults, so the budget must match the operation and objective.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Nested retries can multiply attempts and worsen the dependency outage.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Unbounded waits turn a downstream delay into caller resource exhaustion.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Empty success is a silent correctness failure.

items.prompt: Multiple consumers read an event stream, and one consumer is deployed before the event producer. Which contract protects rollout?
constraints: Consumers may be deployed independently.
Old and new event shapes may coexist.
Unknown fields should not break existing consumers.

options.text: Use versioned, backward-compatible event schemas, tolerant readers, validation, and a producer or consumer rollout order that preserves both versions.
Change the event shape in place and assume every consumer deploys at the same instant.
Delete old events so consumers cannot encounter a prior schema.
Let each consumer infer field meaning independently without a published contract.

feedback.Reason: Distributed consumers need an explicit compatible event contract because deployment and replay are not instantaneous.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Schema versioning and tolerant readers allow old and new producers and consumers to coexist while events remain replayable.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team adds fields compatibly, validates events, and removes old versions only after consumer migration evidence.
Details.errorCorrection: Synchronized deployment is fragile, deleting history destroys recovery, and inference creates divergent interpretation.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Maintaining compatibility versions adds transition complexity but protects independent deployment and replay.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Independent deployments cannot assume an instantaneous all-consumer upgrade.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Deleting history removes replay and recovery options.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Unpublished interpretation makes consumer behavior inconsistent and untestable.

items.prompt: A recovery process must restore a database to a known point without overwriting the source. Which pattern is appropriate?
constraints: The source must remain available or preserved.
Recovery needs a defined point in time.
The restored copy must be validated before promotion.

options.text: Restore a backup or snapshot to a separate recovery resource, validate data and application behavior, and promote it only through a controlled recovery decision.
Restore directly over the production source before checking data integrity.
Use a cache snapshot as the transactional recovery source.
Change the recovery timestamp after restore so any result appears current.

feedback.Reason: A separate immutable recovery point preserves the source and allows validation before the recovered copy becomes authoritative.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Backups or snapshots provide a point-in-time artifact; separate restore and promotion create a controlled recovery boundary.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team checks data completeness, migrations, credentials, and application queries before changing routing or write authority.
Details.errorCorrection: Overwriting before validation can destroy the source, caches are not transactional backups, and timestamps do not alter data truth.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Separate recovery resources cost more but reduce destructive recovery errors.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Direct overwrite removes the ability to compare or recover the original source.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Cache snapshots do not provide a complete transactional recovery point.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Changing metadata does not make stale or incomplete data current.

items.prompt: Several Regions use configuration copied manually, and one Region has a different timeout that causes failover instability. What should replace this path?
constraints: Configuration is part of runtime behavior.
Regions must be intentionally different only where required.
Changes need audit and rollback.

options.text: Manage versioned configuration as code or through a controlled configuration service, validate it per Region, and detect drift before promotion or failover.
Keep regional manual differences because independent operators can react faster during incidents.
Store configuration only in one Region so every failover uses one canonical file even when that Region is down.
Change all timeouts randomly until the Regions fail over at the same time.

feedback.Reason: Versioned and validated configuration removes unintentional regional drift while preserving deliberate differences.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Infrastructure as code or a controlled configuration service records versions, approvals, validation, and regional rollout.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team tests the secondary with the exact configuration it will use and can roll back a bad change.
Details.errorCorrection: Manual divergence is hard to audit, a primary-only file is a recovery dependency, and random tuning is not engineering evidence.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Regional configuration may legitimately differ for quotas or endpoints, but the difference should be explicit and tested.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Manual differences can be accidental, unaudited, and inconsistent during recovery.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A recovery Region cannot depend on a configuration file in the failed Region.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Random tuning can worsen instability and provides no repeatable behavior.

items.prompt: Two distributed services use different timeout units and clocks, causing one to retry after the other has already committed. Which control helps?
constraints: Requests cross service boundaries.
Timeout and retry semantics differ today.
The operation has side effects.

options.text: Define an end-to-end deadline and idempotency contract, propagate remaining time explicitly, and use bounded retries that honor the business operation state.
Increase every service timeout independently because longer waits reduce all distributed failures.
Use local wall-clock timestamps as the only ordering authority across Regions.
Retry a timed-out side effect without an operation key because the first response was not received.

feedback.Reason: Distributed deadlines and idempotency prevent a caller from repeating work after a side effect may already have committed.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A propagated deadline bounds the request while a stable operation key lets the owner return or detect the committed result.
Details.scenarioApplication: Services stop or reject work when the deadline is exhausted and a retry checks the durable operation state.
Details.errorCorrection: Independent longer timeouts can exhaust resources, clocks are not a universal ordering authority, and unkeyed retry can duplicate side effects.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Deadline propagation requires shared conventions and error mapping but reduces cascading timeout failures.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Longer independent waits can increase resource exhaustion and violate the caller's objective.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Wall clocks can skew and do not define business ordering by themselves.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A timeout is ambiguous; a stable operation key is needed for safe retry.

items.prompt: A recovery runbook contains manual commands that differ between operators and have never been executed. Which improvement gives the most confidence?
constraints: The runbook must be repeatable.
Operators need least-privilege access.
The recovery path must be tested without depending on one person.

options.text: Automate deterministic recovery steps with versioned infrastructure, controlled roles, preflight checks, observability, and regular restoration or failover exercises.
Add more prose to the runbook but keep every command manual and untested.
Give all operators administrator access so any recovery command will work.
Run the recovery only during a real outage because rehearsals consume capacity.

feedback.Reason: Repeatable automation and rehearsal turn a recovery document into an executable, observable capability.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Versioned automation, least-privilege roles, preflight checks, and tests expose missing dependencies before a real outage.
Details.scenarioApplication: A second operator can execute the path and compare measured RTO, integrity, and rollback behavior with the objective.
Details.errorCorrection: More prose does not remove command drift, administrator access increases risk, and waiting for a real outage is unsafe.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Automation and exercises cost engineering time but materially reduce recovery uncertainty.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Untested manual steps remain ambiguous and operator-dependent.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Broad access increases blast radius and does not prove repeatability.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: The first real outage is too late to discover a broken runbook.

items.prompt: Which evidence best supports an immutable distributed architecture claim?
constraints: The design spans replaceable compute and multiple components.
Recovery and rollback are in scope.
The evidence must include state and operational behavior.

options.text: Show versioned artifacts, repeatable deployment or recovery, idempotent and bounded distributed operations, compatible state migration, observability, and a controlled failure or rollback test.
Show that the fleet uses containers or images, without testing replacement or rollback.
Show that every component has a different name, which proves distribution and independence.
Show a successful deployment in a healthy environment and infer disaster recovery readiness.

feedback.Reason: Immutability and distribution are architectural behaviors that must be evidenced across deployment, state, failure, and recovery paths.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Artifacts, contracts, retries, state migration, and tests demonstrate whether replacement is safe and repeatable.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team records rollback, replay, failover, and operator evidence rather than treating a container label as resilience.
Details.errorCorrection: Containers alone do not prove immutability, names do not create independent failure domains, and normal deployment does not prove DR.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The evidence effort is material but prevents false confidence in a distributed design.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: An image or container can still be mutable or unsafe without replacement and rollback evidence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Naming does not establish traffic, state, or failure independence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Healthy deployment does not validate degraded recovery or disaster behavior.
